Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-11
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Derek O'Neal (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Redwood), Anika Rao (CTO - Cobalt), Luis Martinez (Lead ML Eng), Priya Singh (PM), Tom Bauer (Security/Infra)

Summary:
Quick technical+commercial intake to understand Cobalt's per-token cost sensitivity, pilot scope, and whether Hosted, Dedicated, or Private is the right initial path. Customer is health-tech (PHI adjacent), wants clarity on unit economics, batching/caching levers, residency/KMS and an eval plan.

Topics covered:
- Current architecture and traffic profile
- Per-token pricing targets and burn ceilings
- Batching, prefix/KV cache impacts and expected gains
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (SLA, residency, cost)
- Security requirements (KMS, audit logs, SSO)
- Pilot scope and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: alright thanks everyone for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, i'll kick us off and then Derek will walk through a couple of numbers. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Anika Rao: good thanks, uh we're excited to see how we can get inference into our triage pipeline, so wanted to do a quick intake on costs and compliance.
[00:15] Luis Martinez: yeah mostly cost per inference is the gating factor; we have a budget cap for Q3 and need to understand burn.
[00:22] Derek O'Neal: cool, i'll try to keep the econ part practical — we can show a model for per-call token counts, batching, and caching levers and the impact on tokens used.
[00:30] Priya Singh: quick note, timeline wise we want a pilot by end of June if possible, else it's pushed to Q4.
[00:36] Maya Chen: good to know — okay Derek?
[00:38] Derek O'Neal: yep, so first, can you confirm current traffic shape — Luis? QPS, typical prompt length, and percent of requests that are chat vs single-shot?
[00:47] Luis Martinez: baseline is about 12 QPS, spikes to 60 during batch ingest windows, average prompt around 120 tokens, responses 200 tokens, so roundtrip 320 tokens on average. about 70% single-turn scoring, 30% multi-turn dialogs.
[01:05] Derek O'Neal: great — and do you have strict latency SLOs? p95?
[01:09] Luis Martinez: yes, p95 350ms is our target for user-facing features; for async triage it's more flexible up to 1.5s.
[01:16] Maya Chen: and can you share on residency / PHI handling — are you okay with Redwood Hosted with encryption-at-rest and SOC2, or do you need a Private VPC/on-prem?
[01:25] Tom Bauer: short answer: we need encryption + customer-managed KMS and audit logs. plus some data residency constraints — certain datasets can't leave our VPC. so hosted-only will be tricky unless there's a Private option.
[01:38] Anika Rao: ideally we want to start with Hosted for speed, but need an easy migration path to Private or Dedicated to satisfy compliance.
[01:47] Derek O'Neal: that's a common pattern — start hosted to move fast, then dedicated or private for residency. cost-wise: hosted has lowest onboarding friction but unit price can be higher than dedicated if you hit high sustained throughput. however batching and KV caching can shrink per-token costs a lot.
[02:03] Maya Chen: let's walk through a quick worked example — Derek, you had a slide?
[02:06] Derek O'Neal: yes — imagine average 320 tokens per request. If you do naive single-shot requests on hosted, at our list rate you'd pay approx X cents per 1k tokens (note: X replaced during follow-up email). but if you enable batching with continuous batching at 50ms window and get 3x effective amortization you can reduce compute tokens by roughly 40-60% depending on overlap. KV cache for multi-turn can drop repeated prefix tokens by up to 70% for long dialogs.
[02:35] Luis Martinez: that caching stat sounds optimistic — how brittle is it? we have a lot of short-lived sessions.
[02:41] Derek O'Neal: fair — KV cache helps for reuse across the same session or similar user workflows. for ephemeral sessions benefit is lower; but prefix caching for repeated system prompts and instruction tokens helps across both.
[02:53] Priya Singh: can we map that to our 12 QPS baseline? like expected token burn reductions?
[02:58] Derek O'Neal: yes — rough calc: baseline 12 QPS * 320 tokens * 3600 seconds = ~13.8M tokens/hour. With batching + KV caching we estimate a 45% reduction -> ~7.6M tokens/hour. multiply by hosted per-token price to get spend; for dedicated you'd provision GPUs and look at $/GPU-hour divided by effective tokens served, which usually drives unit price lower at sustained load.
[03:23] Anika Rao: can you clarify the math on dedicated — we don't want to overprovision and waste money.
[03:28] Derek O'Neal: absolutely — dedicated is best when you have predictable sustained QPS. we model throughput per GPU under your workload (sequence lengths, model size, batching). if your sustained average after optimizations is above the burst threshold we recommend a commit. we'll provide a sizing + cost model in the follow up.
[03:42] Tom Bauer: on security: how do we get customer-managed KMS in hosted? or is that only for Private?
[03:48] Maya Chen: Hosted supports envelope encryption and we can integrate with some KMS providers but customer-managed KMS and HSM-backed keys are typically part of Private deployments for full control. we'll include details in the docs.
[04:00] Luis Martinez: what about lower precision (quantization) to reduce GPU memory and cost — is that something Redwood handles transparently?
[04:06] Derek O'Neal: yes we have quantization-friendly execution paths and can serve quantized variants of models; there are tradeoffs on perplexity/quality but for many scoring tasks 4-bit or 8-bit works well. we'll run a quick quality check with your prompts in the pilot.
[04:18] Priya Singh: competitive question — we also looked at Anthropic and Eigen-hosted; why Redwood versus them on cost?
[04:23] Maya Chen: two things: we focus on production economics — batching, KV cache, and routing policies are built to reduce per-token compute; and we provide a migration path to dedicated/private without changing the API or rollout controls, so you don't re-engineer later. also we'll share benchmark numbers for your prompt set.
[04:38] Anika Rao: good. question on SLA — if we go dedicated what are uptime and latency guarantees?
[04:43] Derek O'Neal: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets (we'll share exact numbers in the contract), plus priority capacity and fallback policies to hosted variants if needed as a safety net.
[04:55] Luis Martinez: fallback sounds risky for PHI, though — we'd need to ensure no data leaves our region.
[04:59] Tom Bauer: exactly, fallback to hosted is not acceptable for PHI.
[05:03] Maya Chen: understood — we'll mark fallback to hosted as disabled for any PHI workloads; Dedicated/Private can be configured to avoid cross-region fallbacks.
[05:12] Luis Martinez: another nit — can you describe token metering accuracy? we had variance in another vendor and billing disputes.
[05:18] Derek O'Neal: Redwood provides token-level accounting and per-route breakdowns in the Console; audit logs and raw request/response hashes can be exported for reconciliation. we also expose per-request token counts in our API responses.
[05:30] Priya Singh: ok that's helpful. what about pilot scope — what would you recommend for a 6-week evaluation?
[05:35] Derek O'Neal: typical pilot: 2-3 models (one smaller for latency-sensitive flows, one larger for quality), host on Hosted first with performance tests, run a 1-week steady-state throughput test to estimate dedicated sizing, and a small Private deploy dry-run (if needed) to validate KMS/audit integrations.
[05:49] Anika Rao: sounds reasonable. budget cap for pilot — we have a $25k allotment for vendor pilots this quarter. can you run the pilot within that?
[05:58] Maya Chen: yes we can design a scoped pilot to fit; we'll size it and show expected token burn and costs in the pricing sheet.
[06:05] Luis Martinez: for the steady-state tests, can we control batching windows from our side? i.e., we want to test with 10ms vs 50ms batching to measure latency vs cost tradeoffs.
[06:13] Derek O'Neal: yes — batching policies are configurable; we'll run the same workload across different batching configurations and report cost/latency curves.
[06:20] Tom Bauer: also need to confirm SSO/SAML and SCIM for provisioning.
[06:24] Maya Chen: yep we support SSO/SAML and SCIM for provisioning; for Private we can do federated identity into your IdP. will include the integration steps.
[06:33] Priya Singh: what about observability and per-token cost breakdowns? our finance team will demand a clear mapping.
[06:38] Derek O'Neal: Redwood Console exposes token-level spend by route/model and you can tag requests to attribute spend to product areas; we'll provision a dashboard for your pilot.
[06:47] Anika Rao: lovely. ok can we deep-dive on the math a little? what assumptions go into the 45% reduction number?
[06:55] Derek O'Neal: it's a combination — 1) batching amortization (reduces per-token kernel overhead), 2) prefix/KV cache re-use across requests, and 3) model-level optimizations like quantized execution. For your mix (70% single-turn, 30% multi-turn), caching mostly helps the 30% and batching helps both. we'll put a workbook with adjustable parameters so you can input your prompt distribution.
[07:17] Luis Martinez: can you outline the workbook inputs we need?
[07:20] Derek O'Neal: prompt and response token histograms, QPS profile over time, percent multi-turn and average session length, target latency SLOs, and whether you require KMS/HSM for the pilot.
[07:31] Anika Rao: we'll pull that together.
[07:33] Priya Singh: one more question — do you support partial residency (i.e., keep embeddings in our VPC but inference hosted)?
[07:40] Maya Chen: yes, hybrid patterns are supported; you can encrypt and store vectors in your VPC while using hosted models, but for PHI we usually recommend Private to avoid egress. we'll detail hybrid patterns in the follow-up.
[07:52] Luis Martinez: regarding model variants — do you offer cheaper smaller models for routing low-value requests?
[07:57] Derek O'Neal: yes routing policies can route lower-cost models for webhooks or low-SLO tasks and route high-SLA requests to larger models; that reduces average unit cost.
[08:06] Tom Bauer: what about audit logs retention — how long are they kept?
[08:10] Maya Chen: by default 90 days, with add-ons for longer retention. Private customers can set retention policies aligned with their compliance.
[08:17] Anika Rao: ok great.
[08:19] Derek O'Neal: quick live example — when we ran your prompt set in a recent baseline with a similar company, switching from naive single-shot to batching + prefix caching reduced billed tokens by about 38% and latency increased by ~120ms at p95 with a 50ms batching window. for non-interactive backfill you can push batching to 200ms and save more.
[08:41] Luis Martinez: can I see the raw baseline numbers in the follow up?
[08:44] Derek O'Neal: yes, we'll attach the workbook and a CSV of the per-prompt token counts.
[08:49] Priya Singh: any gotchas on billing — e.g., if we enable caching, do you charge for cached tokens?
[08:55] Maya Chen: caching reduces billed input tokens because repeated prefixes are not re-sent to the model; you are billed for the tokens actually executed by the model. we'll include precise billing logic in the docs.
[09:05] Anika Rao: great. switching to procurement — what contract flexibility is there for pilots?
[09:09] Maya Chen: pilots are usually month-to-month with capped spend; we can do an MSA for enterprise customers and a short pilot addendum. procurement will see standard SaaS terms plus optional add-ons for Private.
[09:20] Tom Bauer: we need indemnities and clarity on PHI handling.
[09:24] Maya Chen: we'll loop in legal and share redlined examples; Redwood has enterprise security addendums.
[09:30] Luis Martinez: ok next steps?
[09:32] Maya Chen: action items we captured: we'll send pilot pricing and the workbook by Thursday 5/14; Derek will prepare batching/KV examples; Tom will share compliance list; Luis will send the prompt sample. we'll book the performance test tentatively for week of 5/18.
[09:46] Priya Singh: timeline noted. thanks all.
[09:48] Anika Rao: thanks everyone, bye.
